title: esp32c3: calling ticks_us() for >=32 times will cause hang when IRQ is disabled
body:
### Port, board and/or hardware

esp32c3

### MicroPython version

up to commit f1bdac375240941edfc0aa04b646dc3c53d6b371

### Reproduction

st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
tm_til = ticks_us()+1000
while ticks_us()<tm_til: pass
machine.enable_irq(st_irq)

### Expected behaviour

The program can run both with and without IRQ disabled (i.e., with and without the 1st and 4th line).

### Observed behaviour

Without disabling IRQ (by removing the 1st and 4th line), the program can run. However, with IRQ disabled, the program crashes due to WDT timeout, and system restarts.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I cannot replicate it.
`state=machine.disable_irq();machine.enable_irq(state)`
works.
MicroPython v1.24.0-preview.309.gf1bdac375 on 2024-09-14; Generic ESP32 module with ESP3
and
MicroPython v1.24.0-preview.309.gf1bdac375 on 2024-09-14; ESP32C3 module with ESP32C3

You missed to submit the IRQ state returned by disable_irq() in the call to enable_irq(). See the example at
https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/machine.html#machine.disable_irq

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Sorry, I mean the following:
```
def g_dbg1():
	print('start')
	st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
	tm_til = ticks_us()+1000
	while ticks_us()<tm_til: pass
	machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
	print('stop')

def g_dbg2():
	print('start')
	tm_til = ticks_us()+1000
	while ticks_us()<tm_til: pass
	print('stop')
```

`g_dbg2()` will always run(). However, in the master commit firmware, `g_dbg1()` will always crash with WDT timeout. By default, `CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT_TIMEOUT_MS` is set to 300ms, however, even waiting for 1ms (1000us) will cause it to crash. In my application, I am emulating remote controller pulses with recorded intervals.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Confirmed. It works on a genuine ESP32, but fails on a ESPC3. Using the script below it works up to a value of >290000 (= 290ms), and reboots at 300000. But it fails when sleep_us() is replaced by sleep_ms() even with a value of 1.
```
from time import ticks_us, sleep_ms, sleep_us
import machine

def g_dbg1(t=100000):
    print('start')
    st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
    sleep_us(t)
    machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
    print('stop')

def g_dbg2():
    print('start')
    tm_til = ticks_us()+1000
    while ticks_us()<tm_til: pass
    print('stop')
```

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Thanks @participant1 for testing and confirming!
It reboots at 300000us because by default `CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT_TIMEOUT_MS` is set to 300, i.e., 300ms or 300000us or 0.3s. I can easily change `CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT_TIMEOUT_MS` and rebuild. This is of no problem. The problem is that In my context, I cannot use `sleep_us(t)` or `sleep_ms(t)` as the time lapse due to code execution can be significant. Strangely, `ticks_us()` stops advancing after a while when IRQ is disabled.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I tried a variant using a busy loop instead of calling ticks_us() or sleep_us() and toggled a Pin to tell, how fast the WDT fires. It was after like 85µs with that code and exactly for n=30.
```
def g_dbg1(n=10):
    p=machine.Pin(3, machine.Pin.OUT, value=0)
    print('start')
    st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
    p(1)
    i = n
    while i > 0:
        i -= 1
    p(0)
    machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
    print('stop')
```
Interestingly, if I change that code to add a `sleep_us()` into the while loop, the time is multiplied by the delay time of that sleep call, and the WDT fires still at 30 iterations of that loop. So if I call `sleep_us(1000)` in the loop, it fires after about 30ms.

Beside that, the WDT event that happens is `ESP_RST_INT_WDT`, the interrupt watchdog.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I tried one step further and found one closer cause:
```
def g_dbg3(n:int):
	print('start')
	st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
	a=[ticks_us() for i in range(n)]
	machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
	print('stop')
	print('a=',a)
```

Being even more ridiculous:
```
def g_dbg3(n:int):
	print('start')
	st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
	a=[i for i in range(n)]
	machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
	print('stop')
	print('a=',a)
```

Being most ridiculous:
```
def g_dbg3(n:int):
	print('start')
	st_irq = machine.disable_irq()
	for i in range(n): pass
	machine.enable_irq(st_irq)
	print('stop')
```

All the above 3 give the same result. It seems that **while IRQ is disabled, calling `ticks_us()` or any function or any operator for >=32 times will cause hang and trigger WDT reset** after `CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT_TIMEOUT_MS=300ms`. I also tried to set `CONFIG_ESP_INT_WDT=n`, and it will hang forever.

comments.body:
The 32 times bit is probably related to this: https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/8feb714b4d6bc29af3221c0abd47c4adb754f904/ports/esp32/mpconfigport.h#L87 as when the watchdog is disabled it gets stuck here:

```
#0  0x4038f658 in vPortYield () at /home/participant2/.local/esp-idf-504/components/freertos/FreeRTOS-Kernel/portable/riscv/port.c:327
#1  vPortYield () at /home/participant2/.local/esp-idf-504/components/freertos/FreeRTOS-Kernel/portable/riscv/port.c:310
#2  0x42009c50 in mp_thread_mutex_unlock (mutex=<optimized out>) at /home/participant2/src/micropython/ports/esp32/mpthreadport.c:225
#3  0x403834a6 in mp_execute_bytecode (code_state=code_state@entry=0x3fca7c50, inject_exc=inject_exc@entry=0x00000000 <mp_obj_base_t *>)
    at /home/participant2/src/micropython/py/vm.c:1361
...
```

So, interrupts are disabled, the scheduler is idle, and the interpreter got out of the GIL, no wonder it's waiting for something that won't happen :)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> @reporter maybe just handle g_irq_state yourself in machine_enable_irq, as you've got no guarantees the interrupt state mask coming in will always be zero on all processors (xtensa _and_ rv32) :)

Is there any predefined macros indicating whether the device is single-core or not? I think only on single-core chips, when IRQ is disabled, context switch should be forbidden. A user function disables IRQ typically because it wants to do something time critical, e.g., sending/receiving infra-red/RF433 pulses according to precise time intervals, so it does make sense here not to switch context to some other thread that might introduce non-deterministic time elapses.

You're better off using `CONFIG_IDF_TARGET_ESP32C3` (and `CONFIG_IDF_TARGET_ESP32C6`) to limit the extent of your changes.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
> I have a question. On a N-core chips, does it run N interpreters threads, one for each core?

I believe there's only one interpreter, pinned to a single core.  See `app_main` in `ports/esp32/main.c`.  Threads are also spawned on the same core as the interpreter (check out `mp_thread_create_ex` in `ports/esp32/mpthreadport.c`).

That is a true single-core Xtensa MCU, and is not emulating a single-core execution environment as in the case I tested. I'd argue it could still be, though.

One would expect that code that doesn't use model-specific peripherals or CPU-specific registers should behave the same regardless whether it is running on an Xtensa or on a RISC-V CPU.  If nothing else changes on your end except the MCU model you're building for and you see different behaviours, maybe the issue it's not exactly on your end (you still have to deal with it though).

Maybe reproducing the issue outside MicroPython could help to see if there's something MicroPython does that triggers the issue or not.  In the former case you've got more data to eventually figure out a cleaner fix, in the latter case you've got a minimal test case to create an issue on ESP-IDF with.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed report and investigations, @reporter! I've submitted a candidate fix in the linked PR, please take a look.

> the author reported that the irregular time interval occurs only on MicroPython above v1.20, so what changes after v1.20 leads to this bad behaviour? I think the root cause is not addressed.

The change is because the FreeRTOS kernel doesn't guarantee to context switch if task A releases a lock that task B is blocked on, where A and B have equal priority - and the GIL is a lock like this. Runtime may have been more equal in earlier FreeRTOS versions, but this is just was an implementation artifact not by design. The PR #15476 has some more explanation.

> One would expect that code that doesn't use model-specific peripherals or CPU-specific registers should behave the same regardless whether it is running on an Xtensa or on a RISC-V CPU.

The catch is that MicroPython was calling a "from ISR" port layer API to disable interrupts. My view is this breaks the "contract" between the FreeRTOS application and the kernel, because the kernel no longer knows it's in a critical section even though it is. On Xtensa this changes nothing, but on RISC-V it lead to the hang if you do this and then call `taskYIELD()`.

> However, ESP-IDF v5.2.2 results in much lesser free heap than v5.0.4 (30k+ vs 50k+) on exactly the same MicroPython webserver (I reflashed the MicroPython firmware only, all .mpy and config files are left unchanged).

That's a big difference! I think this is less bad than it seems, though - the difference is fragmentation not free heap.

ESP-IDF V5.0.4 on C3:

```
>>> micropython.mem_info()
stack: 516 out of 15360
GC: total: 64000, used: 1584, free: 62416, max new split: 147456
 No. of 1-blocks: 29, 2-blocks: 7, max blk sz: 18, max free sz: 3888
```

ESP-IDF V5.2.2:

```
>>> micropython.mem_info()
stack: 484 out of 15360
GC: total: 64000, used: 1584, free: 62416, max new split: 114688
 No. of 1-blocks: 29, 2-blocks: 7, max blk sz: 18, max free sz: 3888
```

This looks bad ("max new split" is much lower on 5.2.2), but "max new split" is showing the largest single free chunk of RAM, and there is often more than one large free chunk. If we measure the total free RAM for both then it's really close:

5.0.4:

```
>>> import esp32
>>> sum(h[1] for h in esp32.idf_heap_info(esp32.HEAP_DATA))
163256
```

5.2.2:

```
>>> import esp32
>>> sum(h[1] for h in esp32.idf_heap_info(esp32.HEAP_DATA))
163284
```

... if you have another measurement that looks different, or some code that runs out of memory on V5.2.2 but works fine on V5.0.4 then please open a new issue with the details.
